docs.title: ClusterSound
docs.text:
Classify, explore in 3D and put your sample library to work. A desktop app for macOS and Windows that analyses a folder of audio samples, assigns every file to a sound class — kick, snare, hat, 808, pad… — and shows the whole library as a 3D cloud where similar sounds sit close together. From there you build kits, grooves and progressions and take them into Ableton Live. Everything runs locally and your files are never modified.

Install Manual How it works

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Library — 34 classes, subgroups of similar sounds, t-SNE 3D map, Find similar, corrections that teach the classifier. →
  • Store — free samples and packs from Freesound, Openverse, Internet Archive and ccMixter, filtered by instrument and licence. →
  • Recorder — records the audio output, slices on transients, separates stems and restores compressed audio with AI. →
  • Sequencer — 191 grooves in 47 genres to try samples, layers, arrangement and export for Ableton. →
  • Drum Rack — kits of similar samples for an 8×8 Launchpad and a Roland SPD-SX. →
  • Compose — progressions from a chord pack with harmonic suggestions, variations, generated melodies and bass lines. →

docs.title: AI models
docs.text:
ClusterSound uses four models, all local: the audio never leaves the computer and no external service is contacted (the network is only used to download the weights of the extras once).

docs.title: Architectural choices
docs.text:
• No framework for the analysis. YAMNet is rewritten in numpy (convolutions as BLAS matmuls, BatchNorm folded into the weights). Compared to TensorFlow or onnxruntime (~70 MB on its own) the app stays small, starts fast and has no native dependencies to ship.
  • A generic model + a small network trained on your data. YAMNet does not know "closed hat" or "808": its representations, however, separate these sounds well. An MLP head turns the embedding into the 34 classes; a second head self-trains on every library using the file names (and your corrections) as labels.
  • Explicit fusion, not a black box. Name, YAMNet zero-shot, acoustic rules and heads are summed in log-probability with fixed weights tuned with tools/evaluate.py: every signal can be inspected and the system degrades gracefully when one is missing (e.g. files without a name).
  • Heavy models isolated. PyTorch is an extra; Apollo runs in a separate process that ends when the job is done, giving all the memory back; Demucs is imported only when a separation starts. Both work in blocks with a crossfade, for constant memory, progress and cancellation.
  • Automatic device. paths.torch_device() picks CUDA, then Apple MPS, then CPU; if an operation is missing on the GPU, the job goes on on the CPU.

docs.title: Apollo (Enhance)
docs.text: Apollo (Kai Li, Yi Luo, 2024; CC BY-SA 4.0 licence) is a network for the restoration of compressed music: it rebuilds the high frequencies cut by the codecs and softens the artefacts of MP3 and streaming. About 16.6 M parameters, 66 MB of weights.

docs.title: Architecture (enhance/apollo_net.py)
docs.text:
Apollo works in the time-frequency domain with a band-split approach:

flowchart LR
  A["STFT<br/>20 ms"] --> B["80 sub-bands<br/>→ 256 channels"]
  B --> C["6 × BSNet<br/>Roformer + ICB"]
  C --> D["Complex mask<br/>per band"] --> E["iSTFT"]
  1. STFT at 44.1 kHz with a 20 ms window (882 samples, hop 441).
  2. Band split: the spectrum is split into 80 sub-bands; for each one the normalised real/imaginary parts and the log-power go through RMSNorm and a Conv1d to 256 channels.
  3. 6 BSNet blocks, each with:
    • a non-causal Roformer across the bands (attention with RoPE, 8 heads, window 100, MLP with SiLU gate), which models the relations between regions of the spectrum (how to rebuild the highs from the lows);
    • an ICB along time: 3 residual blocks with depthwise conv k=7, RMSNorm, 1×1 with ×4 expansion, SiLU.
  4. For every band RMSNorm → Conv → GLU produce a complex mask/estimate; the iSTFT rebuilds the audio.

The code is a self-contained adaptation of the original: the checkpoint is loaded with torch.load(weights_only=True) and inert stubs for the serialised configuration classes, without running arbitrary code from the file.

docs.title: Isolated execution
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant App
  participant W as Worker (process)
  App->>W: python -m clustersound.enhance.worker IN OUT
  W-->>App: {"progress": 0.3} (one JSON line per event)
  W-->>App: {"done": "OUT"}

docs.title: Processing (enhance/worker.py)
docs.text:
Aspect Choice Resampling to 44.1 kHz with soxr VHQ Blocks 2 s, with 0.5 s of context per side (discarded) and a 50 ms linear crossfade Channels one at a time (half the memory) GPU memory MPS/CUDA cache emptied after every block Fallback if an operation fails on the GPU, the rest of the job goes to the CPU Output sample rate = max(source, 44.1 kHz); peaks above 0.999 scaled down (no clipping); 24-bit WAV

The result is a new … (enhanced).wav file next to the samples (… (migliorato).wav with the Italian interface), with the same licence or provenance note.

docs.title: Classifier
docs.text:
The classifier (classifier.py) assigns every sample to one of the 34 classes. It is not a single model but the fusion of four independent signals, two of which are neural networks (MLPs) working on top of the YAMNet embedding.

flowchart LR
  N["Name and folders"] --> S1["log-prior<br/>from the name"]
  Y["YAMNet scores"] --> S2["AudioSet<br/>zero-shot"]
  F["Features"] --> S3["acoustic<br/>rules"]
  X["Embedding + profile<br/>+ features (1190)"] --> S4["Base head<br/>Library head"]
  S1 & S2 & S3 & S4 --> SUM["weighted Σ<br/>→ softmax"]

docs.title: Architecture of the heads
docs.text:
Both heads are an MLP with one hidden layer:

\[ \mathbf{x} = [\,\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{1024}\;;\;\mathbf{m}_{144}\;;\;\mathbf{f}_{22}\,] \in \mathbb{R}^{1190} \qquad \mathbf{p} = \operatorname{softmax}\!\Big(W_2\,\operatorname{ReLU}\big(W_1\,\tfrac{\mathbf{x}-\mu}{\sigma} + b_1\big) + b_2\Big) \]
  • \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}\): L2-normalised YAMNet embedding; \(\mathbf{m}\): mel profile (attack spectrum, body spectrum, envelope); \(\mathbf{f}\): the 22 acoustic features (with log1p on the tails).
  • Hidden layer of 256 ReLU units; standardisation with the mean and deviation of the training set.
  • Weights \(W_1, W_2\) saved in float16.

Training (train_head), in pure numpy:

Hyperparameter Library head Base head Optimiser Adam (β 0.9 / 0.999) same Steps × batch 1500 × 256 4000 × 256 Learning rate 3·10⁻³, linear decay in the second half same Regularisation weight decay 10⁻³, dropout 0.2 same Sampling class-balanced (prob. ∝ weight / class size) same Minimum classes ≥ 4 examples per class, at least 2 classes ≥ 8 examples Initialisation He (\(\mathcal{N}(0, 2/d)\)) same

Balanced sampling makes the cost independent of the size of the library: 1500 steps take a few seconds even with tens of thousands of files.

docs.title: Base head
docs.text: Shipped with the app (models/base_head.npz, 0.6 MB, 34 classes), trained with tools/train_base_head.py on about 27,000 labelled samples: a file becomes an example only if its name contains a single strong keyword (score ≥ 0.75), with at most 4000 examples per class. It guarantees a good classification even in a library without meaningful names. If the taxonomy changes, the app refuses to load an incompatible head.

docs.title: Library head (self-training)
docs.text:
Retrained at every classification on the open library. The examples are:

  • the files whose name (not the folders) gives a keyword with score ≥ 0.75 — weight 1;
  • the user's manual corrections — weight 3.

It is the heart of the approach: in a real library many files have clear names (Kick 04.wav) and others do not (A101.wav, sample_23.wav). The head learns how the kicks and snares of that library sound from the named files and recognises them in the anonymous ones. Correcting a sample adds a heavy example and restarts the training in the background: the other classifications update within a few seconds.

docs.title: Output of the heads
docs.text:
Every head produces a bounded additive evidence, so that none can cancel the other signals on its own:

\[ h_c = \operatorname{clip}\big(\log(p_c \cdot k),\,-3,\,2\big) \quad\text{for the trained classes}, \qquad h_c = 0 \text{ otherwise} \]

where \(k\) is the number of classes of the head (\(p_c \cdot k = 1\) is "no preference").

docs.title: The other signals
docs.text:
Name and folders. The tokenizer splits the path on separators, camelCase and letter/digit boundaries; the taxonomy keywords give a score per class (1.0, or less for ambiguous tokens such as cl, op). The file name weighs 1, the folders 0.65 · 0.45 · 0.3 · 0.2 going up. The log-prior is

\[ p_c = \frac{0.15}{K} + 0.85\,\frac{v_c^2}{\sum v^2},\qquad n_c = \big(\log p_c - \log\tfrac{1}{K}\big)\cdot\max v \]

so weak evidence (only a folder) pushes less. Special rules handle "open hat" vs "hat", "808" next to another drum name, generic FX words.

YAMNet zero-shot. \(s = 0.5\,s_{\max} + 0.5\,s_{\text{mean}}\) over the 521 AudioSet scores; for every class the maximum of \(s_i \cdot w_{i,c}\) over the mapped AudioSet classes (e.g. Clap ← Clapping 1.0, Applause 0.6), then \(\log(x + 0.02)\).

Acoustic rules. Sigmoid-shaped additive priors computed from the features: low-end energy (kick, 808, tom vs bass), decay and T60 (closed vs open hat, crash, tonal tail of the 808), duration (very short clicks, long pads and textures), tonality vs noise, sweep direction (riser vs downlifter). Details in Algorithms › Classification.

docs.title: Fusion and decision
docs.text:
\[ \mathbf{P} = \operatorname{softmax}\big(2.0\,\mathbf{n} + 0.25\,\mathbf{a} + 0.25\,\mathbf{r} + 2.0\,\mathbf{h}_{\text{lib}} + 1.5\,\mathbf{h}_{\text{base}}\big) \]

Without any head (edge case) the weights become \(2.0\,\mathbf{n} + 1.0\,\mathbf{a} + 0.8\,\mathbf{r}\). The weights were tuned with tools/evaluate.py.

  • The class is the argmax if \(P \ge 0.22\), otherwise Unsorted.
  • The top 4 classes are saved as alternatives (shown in the drawer).
  • A manual label always wins (confidence 1.0).

docs.title: Accuracy
docs.text:
tools/evaluate.py hides the name and folders of the files (5-fold cross-validation) and compares the predicted class with the one given by the name. Test library: 4,932 files, 2,845 labelled; the base head was trained on other ~22,000 samples (duplicates excluded).

Scenario All One-shots only Files without a name, but the library holds other files with names (typical case) 72% 77% No names in the whole library (audio + base head only) 57% 65% YAMNet zero-shot + rules only, without heads (reference) 16% —

Files with a meaningful name are almost always classified by their name. The remaining errors are confusions between close classes (snare/clap/rimshot, closed/open hat, bass/synth) and label noise (e.g. "snare roll" inside a drum fill).

docs.title: Demucs (Extract stems)
docs.text: Meta's Demucs separates a track into its sources. ClusterSound uses htdemucs_6s, the 6-source Hybrid Transformer variant: drums, bass, guitar, piano, vocals, other.

docs.title: The model
docs.text: Hybrid Transformer Demucs combines two U-Net branches, one on the waveform and one on the spectrogram, with a cross-domain Transformer in the middle that makes the two representations talk to each other. The time branch preserves the transients (drums), the spectral one the tonal parts; the output is the sum of the two branches for every source.

docs.title: How it is used (sampler/stems.py)
docs.text: Aspect Choice Installation stems extra (demucs>=4.0.1, torch>=2.1) Weights ~55 MB downloaded on first use into models/demucs in the data folder (Hugging Face for demucs ≥ 4.1, redirected torch.hub for 4.0), with a .ready marker; afterwards only from disk, no network Device CUDA → MPS → CPU; if an operation is missing on the GPU the job goes on on the CPU Process inside the app process, in a thread; PyTorch imported only when the separation starts Blocks 60 s with 2 s of overlap and a linear crossfade; inside every block apply_model(split=True, overlap=0.25) Normalisation mean and standard deviation of the mono reference, restored at the output Mono duplicated to stereo for the model, then averaged back Output one 24-bit WAV per stem; can be cancelled between blocks (partial files are removed)

docs.title: Chosen stems and "Other"
docs.text:
The user ticks only the stems they need; all the sources that are not chosen are summed into "Other". This way the files produced always add up to the original (up to the model's error) and nothing is lost.

The stems of the whole recording go into <recording> - stem/, those of a region into ClusterSound Samples/…/stem/, with the same provenance note as the source. The stem names in the files follow the interface language.

docs.title: YAMNet
docs.text:
YAMNet is a Google MobileNet v1 trained on AudioSet (521 sound event classes). In ClusterSound it provides two things:

  • a 1024-dimensional embedding for every sample: the basis of similarity, subclusters, 3D map and of the classification head;
  • scores on 521 AudioSet classes, used as a zero-shot signal (e.g. Snare drum, Hi-hat, Clapping).

docs.title: Log-mel front end (frontend.py)
docs.text:
It reproduces exactly the features of the original model, in numpy:

Parameter Value Sample rate 16 kHz mono Window / hop 25 ms (400 samples) / 10 ms (160), periodic Hann, FFT 512 Mel 64 HTK bands, 125–7500 Hz, log(mel + 0.001) Patch 96 frames × 64 bands (0.96 s), hop of 48 frames (0.48 s)

The signal is first normalised to a 0.9 peak and cut at 10 s; padding guarantees at least one patch.

docs.title: Network (yamnet_np.py)
docs.text:
MobileNet v1 in NHWC layout with TensorFlow "SAME" padding:

  1. standard 3×3 conv, 32 channels, stride 2 (implemented as im2col + matmul);
  2. 13 depthwise-separable blocks: 3×3 depthwise (nine shifts multiplied and summed) + 1×1 pointwise (BLAS matmul), ReLU after each; strides [2,1,2,1,2,1,2,1,1,1,1,1,2,1] on the 14 layers;
  3. global average pooling → 1024-d embedding;
  4. linear layer 1024 → 521 and sigmoid → scores.

BatchNorm is folded into the weights at conversion time (scale = 1/√(var + 1e-4)), so at runtime there are only multiplications and sums. The 70 arrays are saved in float16 (models/yamnet.npz, 6.9 MB) and converted to float32 on load; the model is a singleton loaded at the first analysis and protected by a lock.

The conversion from the original Keras weights (yamnet.h5) is in tools/build_yamnet_npz.py.

docs.title: Pooling over the patches (embedder.py)
docs.text:
A sample produces N patches (processed in groups of 16). So that silence or the tail do not weigh in:

  • every patch has a weight softmax(mean log-mel energy): loud patches count more;
  • embedding and scores_mean = weighted means; scores_max = maximum over the patches.

Embedding, scores and mel profile are saved in float16 in the cache.

docs.title: How they are used
docs.text: Use What Where Zero-shot 0.5·max + 0.5·mean of the scores, mapped onto the classes with weights (e.g. Kick ← Bass drum 1.0, Thump 0.6) Classifier Classification L2-normalised embedding as the input of the MLP heads Classifier Similarity cosine between normalised embeddings (Find similar, Drum Rack) Clustering Structure k-means subclusters and t-SNE map Clustering Profile attack spectrum, body spectrum and envelope derived from the log-mel (144 values) Audio analysis

docs.title: Strategies and algorithms
docs.text:
How ClusterSound makes its decisions: from the signal analysis to the choice of the samples of a kit, from the next suggested chord to the generated melody. Every page names the modules involved and the real constants used in the code.

Function Strategy in one line Page Analysis 22 envelope and spectrum features + mel profile + multi-band onsets Audio analysis Classification name + zero-shot + rules + MLP, fused in log-probability Classification Subgroups k-means per class, k chosen with the silhouette Clustering and map 3D map PCA → 3D t-SNE, landmarks beyond 2500 points Clustering and map Similar cosine on the YAMNet embeddings Clustering and map Drum Rack kits neighbours without duplicates, weighted random choice with temperature, different groups, similar dynamics Drum Rack SPD-SX random configurations bound by playability limits Drum Rack Grooves step patterns with MPC swing, rolls, deterministic layer alternation Sequencer Next chord additive score: function, cadences, bass motion, common notes, voice leading, pack statistics Harmony Variations minimum-distance voicings, weighted reharmonisation, harmonic rhythm Harmony Melody target contour + note choice by score, question/answer phrases Melody Chords from the melody fit score + Viterbi Melody Key Krumhansl-Schmuckler profiles Melody Slices multi-band spectral novelty, peaks above a threshold Recorder and slicing Store parallel federated search, server-side or local filters, labelling by instrument Store

Determinism

Almost everything that is "random" uses an explicit seed (np.random.default_rng(seed), random.Random(seed) or an integer hash): the same choice produces the same result, and the 🎲 / Regenerate buttons change the seed. The exception is Vary in the Sequencer, which uses Math.random.

docs.title: Audio analysis
docs.text: Every file goes through library.analyse_file only once; the result stays in the SQLite cache.

docs.title: Preparing the signal (audio_io.py)
docs.text:
1. Decoding with libsndfile (soundfile): wav, aif, flac, ogg, mp3, caf, w64. At most the first 30 s are read; the channels are averaged into float32 mono, NaNs are zeroed.
  2. Silence trim: start and end below −60 dB relative to the peak are cut, leaving 2 ms before the first useful sample (the attack stays intact).
  3. Resampling with soxr (HQ quality) in two versions: 16 kHz for YAMNet (normalised to a 0.9 peak, at most 10 s) and 32 kHz for the features.

docs.title: The 22 features (features.py)
docs.text:
Group Feature How Duration duration, log_duration after the trim Envelope attack time from 10% to 90% of the peak of the RMS envelope (10 ms window, 5 ms hop) decay20 time to fall by 20 dB from the peak t60 time to −60 dB, extrapolated from the slope if not reached (max 10 s) tail_ratio share of energy after 200 ms from the peak env_slope slope of the envelope in dB/s (only above 0.3 s) Spectrum centroid, rolloff centroid and 85% rolloff, energy-weighted (STFT 2048 / hop 512) flatness spectral flatness on the active bins only (within 50 dB of the frame peak) zcr zero-crossing rate band_sub, band_low, band_lowmid, band_highmid, band_high share of energy in 0–60, 60–250, 250–2k, 2k–6k, above 6k Hz centroid_slope change of log₂ of the centroid over time (sweep) Tonality harmonicity, f0 autocorrelation of the loudest 100 ms (skipping the first 20 ms of transient), search 40–1000 Hz after the first negative minimum Rhythm onset_count, onset_rate, ioi_regularity multi-band onsets (below); regularity = coefficient of variation of the intervals

For the head the long-tailed features go through log1p.

docs.title: Mel profile (144 values)
docs.text:
Derived from the YAMNet log-mel, aligned to the peak of the sound:

  • attack spectrum (0–60 ms after the peak, 64 bands);
  • body spectrum (60–400 ms, 64 bands);
  • envelope at 16 logarithmic instants from 0 to 2 s.

The two spectra are relative to the maximum of the attack spectrum, so they describe the shape regardless of the volume. Together they say "what happens in the hit and what is left afterwards": the difference between a kick and an 808, or between a closed and an open hat.

docs.title: Multi-band onsets
docs.text:
Used to count the hits (Loop type) and to slice on transients:

  1. STFT 1024 / hop 256; power summed in 8 logarithmic bands;
  2. every band in dB, with a floor 35 dB below the loudest band;
  3. novelty = mean of the 3 bands with the largest rise \(\max(0, dB_t - dB_{t-2})\);
  4. frames more than 45 dB below the peak are ignored;
  5. onsets = local maxima with a rise ≥ 9 dB, at least 70 ms apart.

Measuring the rise over a few milliseconds on several bands makes the detector insensitive to the vibrato and beating of sustained sounds, which do not rise by several dB in ~16 ms.

docs.title: Type
docs.text: Type Rule Loop duration ≥ 1.5 s and ≥ 4 onsets; or name/folders with loop tokens (loop, bpm, groove, beat, break, fill, 120bpm…) and duration > 1 s Long/Texture duration ≥ 2.5 s and not a loop One-shot the rest

docs.title: Measures of the drawer (dynamics.py)
docs.text: Computed on the fly on the whole file (up to 30 s) when you open a sample: peak, RMS and crest in dBFS; waveform (min/max over 1000 points); RMS envelope in dB; estimated ADSR — attack from 10% of the peak, sustain = median of the 40–80% stretch after the peak, decay down to 3 dB from the sustain, release from the last point above sustain − 3 dB down to −60 dB; T60; log-mel spectrogram thumbnail.

docs.title: Classification
docs.text: The model part (MLP heads, training, fusion, accuracy) is described in AI models › Classifier. Here the strategy: why four signals and how they complement each other.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
A real sample library is heterogeneous: commercial packs with perfect names (Snare 07.wav), recordings with anonymous names (A101.wav), folders that tell the class (/Kicks/…) or confuse it (/Drum Loops/…), loops, textures. No signal is enough on its own:

Signal Strong when Weak when Name and folders pack names anonymous names, ambiguous names (cl, op, sd) YAMNet zero-shot categories AudioSet knows (snare, clap, guitar) producer distinctions (closed/open hat, kick/808) Acoustic rules clear physical properties (low vs high, short vs long) in-between cases MLP heads always, if they have seen similar examples rare classes

The fusion sums evidence in log-probability: every signal moves the distribution without being able to dominate it, and when a signal is missing (anonymous name → null log-prior) the others decide.

docs.title: Name parser
docs.text:
• Tokenization: separators, camelCase (ClosedHat → closed, hat), letter/digit boundaries (kick04 → kick, 04), plus the joined variants (open hat → openhat).
  • Keywords per class from taxonomy.py, with a lower weight for ambiguous tokens.
  • Context rules:
    • a hat word with "open" → open hat 1.0; without → closed hat 0.8 (and open hat 0.3); "open"/"closed" without a hat word halve the evidence;
    • "808" next to another drum name weighs ×0.2 (it is the TR-808 drum machine, not a sub kick), next to "kick" ×0.6, next to "bass" the 808 wins;
    • generic words ("cymbal", "perc") lose against a specific one in the same name;
    • fx, sfx, transition… give 0.3 to riser, impact, downlifter and noise.
  • Depth: the file weighs 1, the parent folder 0.65, then 0.45, 0.3, 0.2; for every class the maximum is kept.

docs.title: Acoustic rules (features.rule_logits)
docs.text:
Additive priors built with soft sigmoids \(\sigma\big((x-c)/w\big)\), so without hard thresholds:

Rule Effect Energy below 250 Hz \(> 0.55\) + kick, 808, bass, tom; − hat, shaker, cymbals Energy above 6 kHz \(> 0.35\) + hat, shaker, cymbals, tambourine; − kick, 808, bass, tom Decay to −20 dB \(> 0.25\) s + open hat, − closed hat T60 \(> 0.8\) s + crash Low tonal tail (long T60 × harmonic × low) + 808, − kick Thump (low × decay < 0.35 s × attack < 10 ms) + kick, + tom, − bass Duration < 0.12 s + snap, rimshot, woodblock, closed hat Duration > 2 s + pad, noise, riser, downlifter (− if a short one-shot) Tonal (high harmonicity × low flatness) + melodic instruments and vocals Noisy (high flatness) + hat, shaker, snare, clap, noise, riser, crash Sweep (centroid and envelope rising/falling, on long sounds) + riser / + downlifter Slightly slow attack and noisy + clap (several hits within ~40 ms lengthen the attack)

docs.title: Self-training on the library
docs.text: The key idea: the clear names of a library teach how to classify the anonymous files of the same library. Every classification trains a head on the files whose name has a strong keyword (≥ 0.75) and on the manual corrections (weight 3). Since the sounds of a pack resemble each other, the head generalises to the unnamed files much better than the zero-shot (72% against 16% in the evaluation).

docs.title: Unsorted and corrections
docs.text:
Below a 22% probability the class is Unsorted: better an "I don't know" than a confident mistake. Every correction:

  1. saves the label in cache.sqlite (it survives rescans);
  2. updates that sample straight away;
  3. retrains the library head in the background and recomputes classes and subclusters of the whole library;
  4. invalidates the snapshot (the fingerprint includes the labels).

docs.title: Clustering and 3D map
docs.text: Three structures organise the library: the subclusters inside every class, the neighbours of a sample and the 3D map. All of them start from the L2-normalised YAMNet embeddings, so Euclidean distance and cosine are equivalent.

docs.title: Subclusters (clustering.py)
docs.text:
Inside every class the samples are split into groups of similar sounds (e.g. short dry kicks vs long distorted kicks). The Drum Rack and the Sequencer use them to pick "a group of similar samples" and to keep the groups of a kit different.

  1. With fewer than 6 samples: a single cluster.
  2. On a sample of at most 800 items, k = 2 … min(8, n/3) is tried with k-means++ (up to 50 iterations).
  3. Every k is scored with the mean silhouette; the best one is chosen, but only if the silhouette exceeds 0.05: otherwise the class is homogeneous and stays one cluster.
  4. The final k-means runs on all the samples of the class; the clusters are renumbered by size (#1 = the largest).

The silhouette measures how much closer every point is to its own cluster than to the nearest of the others: it is a parameter-free criterion that avoids splitting classes without structure.

docs.title: Similar (kNN)
docs.text: Find similar and the Drum Rack use the cosine similarity \(\hat{e}_i \cdot \hat{e}_j\) between embeddings: the sample itself is excluded and the first k are returned with their percentage. With 70,000 samples it is a single matrix-vector product in numpy.

docs.title: 3D map (projection.py)
docs.text:
Input. For every sample: 30-dimensional PCA of the embeddings (scaled to mean norm 1) concatenated with 0.8 × the class probabilities. The probabilities bring samples of the same class closer without squashing them: the map stays organised by timbre, but the classes form readable regions.

Preview. A 3-component PCA is shown straight away, while the t-SNE is being computed.

3D t-SNE in numpy.

Parameter Value Dimensions input reduced to 30 with PCA → 3 Perplexity 30 (at most (n − 1)/3), β found by bisection (64 iterations), distances normalised on the median Initialisation PCA × 10⁻² + a little noise (stable layout between runs) Iterations 600; early exaggeration 12 for the first 250 Momentum 0.5 then 0.8 Learning rate max(n/12, 50), with adaptive gains (+0.2 / ×0.8)

Landmarks. Exact t-SNE is quadratic in the number of points. Beyond 2500 samples it runs on 2500 random landmarks; every other sample is placed at the mean of its 5 nearest landmarks (in PCA space) weighted by the inverse of the distance, plus a little jitter (0.02 · standard deviation) so that points do not overlap.

Normalisation and cache. The coordinates are centred on the median and scaled so that the 98th percentile of |coordinate| is 50. The layout is saved in the projections table with a SHA-1 key of folder + files.

flowchart LR
  E["Embedding<br/>1024"] --> P["PCA 30"]
  C["Class<br/>probabilities"] --> J["concat<br/>(× 0.8)"]
  P --> J --> T{"n > 2500?"}
  T -- no --> S["3D t-SNE"]
  T -- yes --> L["t-SNE on 2500 landmarks<br/>+ 5-NN interpolation"]

docs.title: Choosing the Drum Rack samples
docs.text: The Drum Rack has to fill groups of pads with samples that are similar to each other but not identical, respecting family, filters and, for the SPD-SX, the playability of the kit. Code: racks/select.py, racks/dynamics_match.py, racks/spdsx.py, masks and auto-fill in api.py.

docs.title: Space and candidates
docs.text:
• Similarity: cosine between normalised YAMNet embeddings.
  • Candidate mask (_rack_mask): same class as the seed (default), the classes of the group's family, or the whole library; one-shots only (default yes); avoid samples already in the kit; for random kits also the folder/pack filter (substring of the path).
  • Pool: the 400 candidates most similar to the seed are considered.
  • Duplicates: a candidate is discarded if its cosine with one already chosen (seed included) is ≥ 0.995 — copies and renamed files do not take two pads.

docs.title: Fill modes
docs.text:
Most similar (neighbours): goes down the ranking and takes the first k non-duplicates.

Random (pick, random mode): builds a pool of the \(\text{count} + \operatorname{round}(v \cdot 5 \cdot \text{count})\) most similar, where \(v \in [0,1]\) is the variation slider (at \(v = 1\) the pool is 6 times the number of pads). Then it draws without replacement with weights

\[ w_i = \exp\!\Big(\frac{s_i - s_{\max}}{T}\Big), \qquad T = 0.05 \]

The low temperature clearly favours the most similar but leaves room for the others; the slider widens the pool. The result is sorted by similarity and reproducible from the random seed (Regenerate changes it).

Manual: the 60 most similar neighbours in a list to tick.

Trail (trail): the stops of Find similar chosen by hand, in order and without repetitions, cut to the size of the group; if they are too few, they are completed with the neighbours of the last stop (the filters only apply to the completion).

docs.title: Random group and random kit
docs.text:
random_group is the building block of 🎲 Random, of the Sequencer's random kit and of Generate kit:

  1. among the allowed candidates the groups class:subcluster are listed;
  2. one is chosen uniformly (not in proportion to its size: small groups come out too);
  3. a random seed inside the group;
  4. the other count − 1 with a random pick around the seed.

rack_randomize applies it to every unlocked group (or only to the empty ones):

  • the samples already used are excluded;
  • with distinct groups (always for the SPD-SX) the subclusters already used by other groups are excluded first, so two rows of hats, or the pedal kick and a pad kick, sound different; if too few candidates are left that way, the constraint is dropped;
  • with similar dynamics the reference is the set of samples already put in the kit (see below).

Auto-fill (rack_autofill) is the deterministic version: for every empty group it picks as seed the best unused one-shot of the family — sorting by class of the family, one-shots first, non-loop names first, decreasing confidence — preferring among the first 300 a subcluster not yet used in the same family; then it completes with a random pick at variation 0.3.

docs.title: Similar dynamics (dynamics_match.py)
docs.text:
A kit sounds cohesive if its hits have compatible envelopes. Every sample has a 5-value envelope vector:

Feature Scale Weight attack log₁₀ 0.7 decay to −20 dB log₁₀ 1.2 T60 log₁₀ 1.2 tail share linear 1.0 envelope slope (dB/s, clipped to [−200, 50]) linear 0.6

The values are standardised within every class (with statistics of the whole library for classes with fewer than 5 samples): this way a kick that is short for a kick comes out close to a hat that is short for a hat. The reference is the mean of the samples already chosen; the distance is the RMS over the 5 dimensions and the score \(\exp(-d^2/2)\). The margin keeps the closest fraction of the candidates (at least 8), which then goes to the random choice.

docs.title: 8×8 layout
docs.text:
• Pads numbered row·8 + column, row 0 at the bottom.
  • Launchpad notes: \(36 + 16q + 4\,(r \bmod 4) + (c \bmod 4)\), with quadrant \(q = 2[r \ge 4] + [c \ge 4]\) → 36–51, 52–67, 68–83, 84–99. Rows notes: \(36 + p\).
  • Layouts: 8 columns of 8, 16 blocks 2×2, 4 quadrants 4×4, 16 columns of 4 (one family per quadrant), free; every layout has default families (18 families in all). Choke is on by default for the hat families.

docs.title: Roland SPD-SX
docs.text:
Pads and triggers: 9 pads (notes 60–68) plus Trig 1 (pedal, 69) and Trig 2 (70). Without the pedal pad 8 becomes a group of its own with the kick; every connected trigger is a group (T1 kick, T2 cymbal).

Playability limits: at most 2 kicks, 3 snares/claps, 5 hats/cymbals. The role of a group comes from its family; for generic families ("any", "fx") the class of the sample on every pad is counted. A family is offered for a group only if, changing it, no role exceeds \(\max(\text{limit}, \text{current count})\).

Generate kit (random_config + rack_randomize):

  1. up to 50 attempts: a random configuration (Free excluded), in which every group swaps its family for a variant of the same role (snare ↔ clap, hat ↔ hat + cymbal, perc ↔ shaker ↔ tom…); T1 stays a kick;
  2. the first one that respects every limit is accepted;
  3. it is filled with distinct groups (above). If a group is locked, or keeping the configuration was asked, only the filling changes.

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
• .adg: gzipped XML from neutral Live 10 templates; one DrumBranch per pad with note (ReceivingNote = 128 − note), choke group and a Simpler in one-shot mode with a path relative to the preset.
  • SPD-SX: also 16-bit / 44.1 kHz WAVs (resampled with soxr) for Wave Manager, named P1…P9, T1 Pedal, T2, plus README.txt with the pad map.

docs.title: Harmony and chords
docs.text: Code: chords/library.py, theory.py, harmony.py, variations.py, perform.py. Chords are not generated from abstract rules: they are the MIDI clips of the chord pack, indexed and then sorted, transposed and varied. This way every chord has a voicing played by a musician.

docs.title: Indexing the pack
docs.text:
• Key from the NN - X Major - Y Minor folders; the mode from the presence of "minor" in the subfolders; the category (triads, extended, borrowed, progressions…) from keywords of the folders.
  • Segmentation: notes with onsets within 1/32 form a chord (resampled to 480 PPQ); every chord lasts until the next one and the end of the file is rounded to the bar. A file with several segments is a progression; the degrees in brackets in the name ((I-V-vi-IV)) are read if they are all valid.
  • Root: from the name of the chord, otherwise from the degree, otherwise estimated (below).
  • Missing keys: served by the nearest key of the pack with the same category, transposing by −6…+5 semitones (on a tie, downwards). The results are marked transposed.
  • Statistics: for every progression the bigrams of degrees are counted (consecutive pairs, repetitions excluded; the last → first return counts 0.5 because progressions loop).

docs.title: Theory (theory.py)
docs.text:
Quality from the intervals above the root: with a major third → augmented (augmented 5th without a perfect one), dominant (minor 7th without a major one) or major; with a minor third → diminished (diminished 5th without a perfect one) or minor; otherwise sus.

Estimated root: for every pitch class r

\[ \text{score}(r) = 2[\text{3rd}] + 1.5[\text{5th}] + 1[\text{dim. 5th with min. 3rd}] + 0.5[\text{7th}] + 0.75[r = \text{bass}] \]

Harmonic function: a chord is diatonic if the root and the triad core (root, 3rd, 5th) are in the scale (in minor the leading tone is allowed too). Diatonic chords have a Tonic, Subdominant or Dominant function by degree; all the others are C (colour / modal borrowing). These are the four colours of the browser.

docs.title: Next chord
docs.text:
For every candidate b after the chord a, transition(a, b) adds up:

Term Value Function flow T/S/D/C table: e.g. T→S 1.0 · S→D 1.0 · D→T 1.0 · T→D 0.75 · D→S 0.3 Cadence (the first that matches) V→I +0.6 · ii→V +0.45 · plagal +0.35 · deceptive +0.35 · bVI→bVII +0.35 · mixolydian bVII→I +0.35 · Neapolitan +0.3 · leading tone→tonic +0.3 … Bass motion fourth up (fifth down) +0.35 · fifth up +0.15 · stepwise +0.15 · tritone −0.3 · same root −0.3 (different colour) or −0.7 Common notes +0.08 per note, up to 3 Voice leading \(\max(0,\;0.3 - 0.03\,d)\), with d = mean distance in semitones Frequency in the pack \(+0.6 \cdot \text{bigram}(a,b) / \max\)

The voice leading distance between two voicings is the mean of two means: every note of b to the nearest note of a, and vice versa.

Then suggest:

  • a −0.8 penalty for the same chord of the library and −0.15 for an A-B-A ping-pong;
  • if there is already a chord n after it, \(0.6 \cdot \text{transition}(b, n)\) is added: the suggestion also has to lead well;
  • without a previous chord, starting score: T 1.0 (+0.4 if it is the I) · S 0.55 · D 0.35 · C 0.2;
  • the candidates are grouped by (root, minor, diminished): the best voicing wins, the others become the colour variants under the proposal;
  • the scores are rescaled between 0.35 and 1 for the bar; the reasons shown are the labels of the terms that fired.

With an unlocked key the candidates include the nearby keys: dominant, subdominant, relative and parallel.

docs.title: Variations
docs.text:
All deterministic given the seed (random.Random(seed)).

Fitting a voicing (_fit): tries inversions −2…+2 × octaves −1…+1 (notes between 24 and 100) and picks the one that minimises \(d(\text{previous}) + 0.15\,|\text{centre} - \text{reference centre}|/3\).

Of a chord:

  • voicing: 1st and 2nd inversion, inverted downwards, drop-2, open (2nd voice an octave up), close, doubled bass; at the top the one with minimal voice leading from the previous chord;
  • colour: same root and same mode from the pack, preferring a different number of notes;
  • substitution: the first 2 of suggest in context (chord before and after) plus 2 random ones among the others.

Of the progression (vary_progression), with How much to vary \(a \in [0.05, 1]\):

Kind Strategy reharmonisation replaces \(\operatorname{round}(a \cdot \text{inner})\) chords (first and last stay); every choice takes rank \(\lfloor u^2 \cdot 5\rfloor\) among the 5 best suggestions, with u uniform: it favours the best without always being the same harmonic rhythm eighth-note anticipation, long-short (1.5 + 0.5), split of a chord ≥ 1 bar with the best suggestion in the second half voice leading chain of _fit for minimal motion richer / sparser same root with more or fewer notes (sparser prefers triads) ending typical cadence of the mode on the last 2 chords (IV→V, bVI→bVII, IV→iv, ii→V…)

The proposals are deduplicated by signature; up to 4× the number requested are generated.

docs.title: Playing (perform.py)
docs.text:
From chords to notes, at 480 PPQ; the same function produces preview, MIDI and clips for Live.

  • Hits: the rhythm grid repeats over the absolute timeline; a length of 0 means "until the next hit". A chord that starts off the grid gets a hit at its start.
  • Swing: odd sixteenths delayed by \((\text{swing}/50 - 1)\cdot 120\) ticks.
  • Strum: guitar direction (down on the beats, up in between), alternate, always up/down; total spread limited to half the length; linear, accelerating \(1-(1-x)^2\) or decelerating \(x^2\) curve; velocity tilt and softer upstrokes; upstrokes can be limited to the top notes.
  • Arpeggio: up, down, up-down, random over 1–3 octaves; off-beat notes at 0.86 of the velocity.
  • Dynamics: crescendo \(0.72 + 0.42f\), diminuendo \(1.14 - 0.42f\), bass accent ×1.12; accents on the beats.
  • Deterministic humanize (humanize seed XOR CRC32 of the chord): timing shifts a whole hit together, with a drift that mixes white noise and cosine-interpolated "value" noise (period 2 beats); plus per-note spread, length ±% and velocity ±. Finally overlaps on the same note are shortened and notes under 12 ticks are dropped.

docs.title: Melody
docs.text: Code: chords/melody.py. Every generator gets the chord map (which chord plays on every sixteenth) and the key, is deterministic given the seed and produces several proposals (up to 3× those requested, deduplicated).

docs.title: Melody (lead)
docs.text:
The strategy combines a global contour with a local note-by-note choice, organised in phrases.

Phrases and rhythm.

  • Phrases of 2 bars (high density), 4 (low) or random. The rhythm of every bar is chosen from a repertoire per density.
  • Odd phrases are answers: with probability 0.75 they take up the rhythm of the question, bar by bar; the last bar of the answer is mutated (an onset added or removed).
  • Breath: the last bar of a phrase keeps only the onsets up to the third beat, so the phrase ends on a long note, and that note is the root of the chord.

Candidate pitches. On the strong beats the chord notes; on the weak ones the scale plus the chord notes.

Contour. The centre of attraction within the phrase (position \(x \in [0,1]\)) is

\[ \text{target}(x) = \text{centre} + 0.7\cdot\text{half-range}\cdot f(x) \]

with arch \(f = 1.2\sin(\pi x) - 0.4\), rising \(f = -0.6 + 1.2x\), falling \(f = 0.6 - 1.2x\), wave \(f = 0.6\sin\big(\pi(2x + \varphi)\big)\).

Note choice (_pick): among the candidates the highest score wins:

Term Value distance from the contour (-0.25\, interval from the previous note (a semitones) \(-0.35\,a\) up to 4; beyond \(-1.4 - 0.6\,(a-4)\); beyond the fifth another −3 repeated note −0.9 on the strong beats, −1.6 on the weak ones unrecovered leap −1.5 if after a leap > 4 semitones it does not step back in the opposite direction variety \(+0.9\,u\), u uniform

These are the classic rules of counterpoint (stepwise motion, recovered leaps, few repetitions) in the form of a score. Velocity: 104 on the downbeat, 92 on the beats, 80 elsewhere, ±6.

docs.title: Bass
docs.text:
• The root of every chord, in the octave closest to the previous one and pulled towards the bottom of the range.
  • Styles: roots, octaves, fifths, walking (scale notes towards the next root).
  • Approach: with probability 0.7 the last note before a chord change is ±1/±2 semitones from the next root.

docs.title: Arpeggio
docs.text: The notes of the chord in a 7-note window around the previous one, in steps of 4 / 2 / 1 sixteenths by density, in the rising, falling, up and down, random directions.

docs.title: Riff
docs.text: A one-bar cell of intervals built with _pick on the wave contour; on every chord it is transposed to its root and "snapped" to the chord notes on the beats (scale + chord elsewhere). Every fourth bar the rhythm is mutated, so that the riff is not mechanical.

docs.title: Pad and Keys
docs.text: Close voicings of up to 4 notes (the fifth goes first) chosen for the minimum distance from the previous one. Pad: held (low density), one per bar or one per half bar. Keys: rhythmic comping from a repertoire of rhythms.

docs.title: Chords from the melody
docs.text:
The inverse problem: given a melody, find a progression of the pack that harmonises it.

  1. Candidates: the pack's chords distinct by (root, set of notes), optionally also from the nearby keys.
  2. Segments: one chord per bar, two, or automatic: a bar is split if the best whole chord fits less than 0.7 and the two halves together are worth more than \(2\cdot\text{whole} + 0.3\).
  3. Note weight: length × 1.5 if the note falls on a beat × 2 if it opens the segment.

  4. Fit of a chord to a segment (normalised on the total weight):

    Melody note Contribution chord note \(+w\) in the scale, out of the chord \(-0.15\,w\) out of the scale \(-0.6\,w\) a semitone from a chord note another \(-0.25\,w\) downbeat note = root \(+0.15\) of the total

    minus \(0.03\) for every chord note beyond the third (it prefers simple chords).

  5. Viterbi over the sequence of segments, to choose the best chain and not just the best chord per segment:

    \[ \text{emission} = 2.2\cdot\text{fit},\quad \text{start} = 0.5\cdot\text{start score},\quad \text{transition} = 0.6\cdot\text{transition}(a,b) - 0.5\,[a = b] \]

    with the same transition as the suggestions and a +0.8 bonus if the last chord is the I.

  6. Alternatives: the following versions add Gaussian noise (σ 0.25) and −0.35 for the chords already used in that segment.

  7. Clips: repeated chords merged, voicings chained with _fit around the middle register and lowered by an octave while they sit under the melody.

docs.title: Key detection
docs.text: Krumhansl-Schmuckler algorithm: the histogram of the 12 pitch classes (weighted by length, first and last note count double) is correlated (Pearson) with the major and minor key profiles rotated over the 12 tonics; the highest correlation among the 24 keys wins. It is used when a version has only the melody or for Detect from the melody.

docs.title: Recorder and slicing
docs.text: Code: sampler/recorder.py, capture.py, wasapi.py, native/cs_tap.swift, sampler/slicing.py, sampler/session.py, sampler/export.py.

docs.title: Recording the audio output
docs.text:
The Recorder has to capture what a device plays, several devices together too, without virtual drivers. Every chosen output is a Track with its own backend and its own Writer; they start together and an error on one device does not stop the others (the recording fails only if all of them fail).

Platform Backend How macOS 14.2+ cs-tap Swift helper with Core Audio process taps: it gets the same audio the device plays; it excludes ClusterSound's process (--exclude-pid); it writes a JSON header and then float32 PCM on stdout macOS, without the helper ScreenCaptureKit only All outputs: a minimal mandatory video stream (2×2 px, 1 fps), 48 kHz stereo audio, the app's audio excluded Windows WASAPI loopback (soundcard) one thread per output with its own COM initialisation, 48 kHz, 1024-frame blocks; the "mix" is the default output

The Writer creates the file at the first block (when it knows the channels), maps the channels (mono = mean, stereo, all), resamples in streaming with soxr.ResampleStream if needed and writes with libsndfile (WAV, AIFF, FLAC, CAF, constant-bitrate MP3, OGG, Opus at 48 kHz). M4A goes through an intermediate CAF converted with afconvert. An RMS meter per track feeds the UI.

Protected streams record silence: nothing is decrypted.

docs.title: Slicing on transients
docs.text:
It uses the multi-band onset detector, adapted to long recordings:

  1. Sensitivity → rise threshold: linear from 18 dB (0) to 4 dB (1).
  2. Blocks of 30 s with 1 s of overlap: every block "owns" the interval \([a + 0.5,\; a + \text{hop} + 0.5)\) s, so an onset close to the edge is counted only once; 50 ms of silence are prepended to the first block so that a hit at t = 0 shows a rise. Onsets within 30 ms are merged.
  3. Regions: from 5 ms before the onset (pre-roll) to the next one minus the pre-roll, limited to the maximum length (30 s); every region is then shortened to the last 10 ms RMS window above −50 dB relative to its peak (no silent tails). Regions under 30 ms are discarded.

docs.title: Rendering the samples
docs.text:
When a region becomes a file (slicing.render):

  • the start moves to the nearest zero crossing, at most 2 ms earlier (no clicks);
  • 1 ms fade-in and 10 ms fade-out;
  • optional normalisation to −0.3 dBFS;
  • 24-bit WAV in <samples folder>/<source>/<title>/, with .license.txt (Store links) or .source.txt (recordings: private use). A region already exported and not changed reuses its file.

Sources are limited to 20 minutes (beyond that they are cut and flagged); the waveform is computed as min/max columns with np.minimum.reduceat / np.maximum.reduceat for the visible width.

docs.title: Links
docs.text: links.py recognises Freesound, Internet Archive, ccMixter, Openverse and Wikimedia Commons links and resolves them with the providers' APIs (a ccMixter zip pack is replaced by its preview, because the editor opens a single file); links to streaming services (YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud…) are refused with an explanation.

docs.title: Sequencer and groove
docs.text: Code: patterns/model.py (format and timing), patterns/genres.py (genres), patterns/render.py (audio), patterns/midi.py, patterns/arrange.py, patterns/ableton.py; in JS ui/pattern.js and ui/sequencer.js.

docs.title: The model of a pattern
docs.text:
• Grid: 16 steps per bar, 96 PPQ, so 24 ticks per step (a sixteenth note).
  • Buses: 10 drum buses with one GM note each, plus the Bass bus.
  • Compact notation in the genres: X = 127 (accent), x = 100, o = 55 (ghost), 2/3/4 = roll at velocity 100, . = rest; a string shorter than the pattern is repeated. The bass uses step:length:semitones tokens with g = glide and ! = accent (velocity 120).

docs.title: Swing
docs.text:
MPC-style swing on the odd sixteenths:

\[ \text{tick}(s) = 24\,s + \big[s \text{ odd}\big]\cdot\operatorname{round}\!\Big(\frac{\text{swing}}{100}\cdot 48 - 24\Big) \]

At 50% no shift, at 75% the off-beat sixteenths come 12 ticks later (full shuffle). Sequences keep the swing of every bar (swing_bars).

docs.title: Rolls
docs.text: A ×r roll splits the step into r evenly spaced hits; the k-th has velocity \(v\,(1 - 0.12k)\), so it sounds like a roll and not like a machine gun.

docs.title: Layer alternation
docs.text:
With 2+ layers sharing the steps of the bus, a single layer plays on every hit:

Mode Layer of hit h on step s in turn \(h \bmod n\) random \(\text{hash}(seed, s) \bmod n\) — the same choice on every loop random every loop \(\text{hash}(seed, s + \text{loop}\cdot N) \bmod n\) — a new choice on every repetition

hash is a 32-bit integer hash (multiplication by 2654435761, xor-shift, multiplication by 0x45D9F3B) bit for bit identical in Python (alt_hash) and in JS (altHash): the Web Audio preview, the WAV and the exported MIDI play the same layers. ⚄ changes the seed. Layers with their own steps always play.

docs.title: Genres
docs.text:
Every genre (G) has a typical BPM and range, swing, key, bass octave, an optional half-time and hand-written variants (V: bus steps, bass line, bars). Two variants are derived automatically from the first one:

  • Fill: the last 4 sixteenths of the snare (or the clap) become xx33 (3x33 in half-time genres): a roll on the last beat; a ..xx tom run on the last beat; a crash on the downbeat if the pattern has no cymbals.
  • Breakdown: kick, snare, toms and bass out; if nothing is left, an off-beat hat; an FX hit on the downbeat.

docs.title: Vary
docs.text:
Vary (in pattern.js) applies small idiomatic mutations:

  1. moves an off-beat kick by ±1 sixteenth (if the target step is free), or adds one 6 steps from the end;
  2. adds up to 2 snare ghosts (velocity 55) on free off-beats;
  3. gives a closed hat hit a ×2 or ×3 roll;
  4. with 50% probability, if there is an open hat, turns one on or off on an "and" (step 2 + 4k).

docs.title: Random kit
docs.text: For every bus that plays and is not locked it asks random_refs(classes of the bus, n) — the same random group as the Drum Rack — with n = 1, 2 or 4 (the bass always 1), excluding the samples already chosen. With similar dynamics the reference is the audible layers of the buses that are not regenerated plus those chosen along the way. Buses with several layers switch to random alternation, except kick, FX and bass.

docs.title: Rendering (render.py)
docs.text:
The loop WAV is mixed in numpy, with the same logic as the Web Audio scheduler:

  • Velocity gain \((v/127)^{1.5}\), constant-power pan, volume and pan per bus and layer.
  • Samples loaded up to 30 s, stereo, 44.1 kHz; pitch is a resampling (like a sampler: the length changes too); the offset in ms shifts the layer.
  • Seamless loop: tails that run past the end of the loop come back in from the start.
  • Choke: every open hat is closed (10 ms fade) at the next closed hat, across the loop boundary too.
  • High-pass/low-pass filters per bus: magnitude response of a 2nd-order Butterworth applied in the FFT domain (zero phase).
  • Limiting: if the mix goes above 0.98 it is scaled down.

docs.title: Bass tuning
docs.text:
A bass sample plays in tune because its root note is estimated: 3 s, trim, autocorrelation of the loudest 100 ms (after the transient), search for the fundamental 40–1000 Hz; if the harmonicity is above 0.4 (0.5 for library samples) \(\text{root} = \operatorname{round}\big(69 + 12\log_2(f_0/440)\big)\). Every bass note is then transposed by

\[ 12(\text{octave}+1) + \text{key} + \text{semitones} - \text{root} + \text{layer pitch}. \]

docs.title: MIDI and export
docs.text:
• Dependency-free SMF writer: type 0 or 1, note-offs before note-ons on the same tick.
  • Drum Rack mapping: consecutive notes from 36 for the buses used; an alternating bus gets one pad per layer and every hit goes to the pad of the layer that plays it. GM: one note per bus. Drum notes 1/32 long.
  • Glide: a note with glide overlaps the next one by 1/64 (legato), so the Simpler in mono mode slides.
  • Ableton: Drum Rack with one pad per bus (nested Instrument Rack for the layers, choke on the hats), bass in a mono classic Simpler with RootKey = estimated root, 60 ms release and 60 ms glide when needed.
  • Sequences (arrange.flatten): blocks × repetitions are concatenated into a single pattern (at most 256 bars), with per-bar swing and section boundaries; layers with their own steps are repeated over the whole length.

docs.title: Store
docs.text: Code: online/ (search.py, instruments.py, base.py, cache.py, downloads.py, catalog.py and one module per provider).

docs.title: Federated search
docs.text:
search() queries Freesound, Openverse, Internet Archive and ccMixter in parallel (ThreadPoolExecutor). Errors are per source: a slow or failing source shows its message without blocking the others.

Every provider translates the filters into its own query language:

Source Query Freesound Solr filter tag:(…) + licence, duration, BPM, key, single_event/loopable, file type; for packs group_by_pack=1 Openverse one query per instrument (up to 4) in parallel, results interleaved and deduplicated; sources limited to Freesound and Wikimedia (Jamendo has whole songs, not samples) Internet Archive mediatype:audio + "sample pack" context, MIDI excluded; a declared licence is required unless asked otherwise ccMixter reqtags=sample + instrument tags

Every module declares which filters it applies server-side (SERVER_FILTERS, the FS·OV·IA·CC tags in the UI); all the results go through the local passes() filter anyway (instrument, licence, commercial use, file/pack, type, duration, BPM, key, lossless, suspect packs), so the filters work the same on every source. Packs skip the per-file checks until they are expanded.

docs.title: Labelling by instrument
docs.text:
The sources do not know the 34 classes: every result is labelled with the same name parser as the library (instruments.infer):

  1. if the tags contain non-musical context words (soccer, door, gun…) without musical words, no class;
  2. phrases rewritten into the taxonomy keywords ("bass drum" → kick);
  3. score on the title, or on the path inside a pack (with the decreasing folder weights); the tags count 0.8;
  4. the best class if the score is ≥ 0.45.

A result is kept if its class is in the filter, or if the server already found it for that instrument and it has no non-musical context. The type comes from name, tags and duration (one-shot ≤ 2.5 s, loop if it has a BPM in the title, …); BPM (50–220) and key from the title (the key needs an accidental or the mode word, so that normal words are not read as notes).

docs.title: Suspect packs
docs.text:
A regex of commercial producers (Big Fish Audio, Sound Ideas, Native Instruments, Splice, Loopmasters, Cymatics, Apple Loops, Ableton packs…) and of piracy words (leaked, cracked, warez, torrent) is applied to the title, author and subjects of Internet Archive packs. Files inherit the flag from the pack; suspect ones are hidden unless asked for.

Expanding Internet Archive packs: only original loose files, ZIP contents read from the listing page (4 threads, __MACOSX excluded), duplicates with the same name reduced to the best format (wav > aif > flac > ogg > mp3), at most 3000 files.

docs.title: Cache and licences
docs.text:
• HTTP responses: in-memory cache per URL + parameters + headers, 10 minutes (1 hour for Freesound packs), cleared beyond 500 entries.
  • Audio previews: files named after the SHA-1 of the URL, only from allowed hosts, at most 60 MB each, atomic write; access updates the date (LRU) and prune deletes the oldest beyond the limit (300 MB), except the samples used by the open pattern or rack.
  • Licences normalised into cc0, pd, by, by-sa, by-nd, by-nc, by-nc-sa, by-nc-nd, sampling+, rf, unknown; commercial use = cc0, pd, by, by-sa, rf.
  • Downloads only from allowed hosts, safe names on Windows too, with .license.txt (author, licence, link, attribution) in the interface language.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
The essential procedures, in a few steps. To understand what each screen does go to the Manual; to learn how it works inside, to Technical, AI models and Algorithms.

  • Installation — from source on macOS or Windows, plus the optional extras.
  • First launch — choose the sample folder and let the analysis work.
  • Ableton Live — Max for Live device and Remote Script in three steps.
  • Building the app — ClusterSound.app or ClusterSound.exe.
  • Troubleshooting — permissions, WebView2, logs.

docs.title: Ableton Live
docs.text:
You need Live 10.1 Suite or later (Max for Live). To do only once.

  1. Install the device and the Remote Script into the User Library:

    macOSWindows 
    tools/install_live.sh

    python tools\install_live.py

    If the User Library is not in the default location, pass it as an argument.

  2. Restart Live. In Preferences → Link/MIDI (Settings → Link, Tempo & MIDI in Live 12) choose ClusterSoundBridge as Control Surface, with Input and Output set to None.

  3. Drag the ClusterSound device (browser → Max MIDI Effect) onto a MIDI track.

With the app open the device shows the catalogue; try Send to Live from the Sequencer. Full usage in Max for Live, protocol in Live integration.

Tip

For a self-contained device: open it in Max, Freeze Device, save.

docs.title: Building the app
docs.text:
PyInstaller only builds for the system it runs on.

macOSWindows 
tools/build_app.sh

Result: dist/ClusterSound.app (it also compiles the Recorder's cs-tap helper and the icon, if missing). Distribute only the .app bundle.

powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File tools\build_app.ps1

Result: dist\ClusterSound\ClusterSound.exe. Distribute the whole dist\ClusterSound folder.

Demucs and PyTorch are included only if installed in the build environment. Details on the spec and the native helper in Development and tests.

docs.title: Automatic releases
docs.text:
Pushing a vX.Y.Z tag runs the release workflow (.github/workflows/release.yml): it builds the app on GitHub for Apple Silicon and Intel, with all the extras (midi, capture, stems, enhance), and publishes ClusterSound-X.Y.Z-macos-arm64.zip and ClusterSound-X.Y.Z-macos-x86_64.zip as a GitHub Release.

  1. Set version in pyproject.toml (the bundle reads it from there) and merge develop into main.

  2. Tag the merge on main and push the tag:

    git tag -a vX.Y.Z -m "ClusterSound X.Y.Z" && git push origin vX.Y.Z

The workflow stops if the tag is not on main or differs from the version in pyproject.toml. Run by hand from the Actions tab, it only builds and leaves the zips as workflow artifacts.

The app is signed ad hoc, not notarized: on first launch macOS asks to open it with right-click › Open (or xattr -cr ClusterSound.app).

docs.title: First launch
docs.text:
1. Start the app (python -m clustersound or ClusterSound.app).
  2. In the empty Library press Choose folder… and point to the sample folder (it is read recursively).
  3. Wait for the analysis: the bar at the top shows the phases Finding files → Analysis → Classification → 3D layout. While the map is being computed a preview (PCA) appears straight away, then the final view (t-SNE).
  4. Click a point of the cloud: the sample plays and the detail drawer opens.

Timing

The first analysis uses every core and shows files/s live. The next ones are almost instant: unchanged files come from the cache and, if nothing changed, the whole library is restored from a snapshot.

Your files are not touched

ClusterSound never modifies, moves or renames the original files. Classes, corrections and the map live in the app's data folder.

macOS Windows Data (settings, cache, snapshots, models) ~/Library/Application Support/ClusterSound %APPDATA%\ClusterSound Cache (online previews, helpers) ~/Library/Caches/ClusterSound %LOCALAPPDATA%\ClusterSound\Cache Downloads, Samples, Recordings, Patterns ~/Music/ClusterSound … ~\Music\ClusterSound …

No samples yet? Press Browse the free Store: see Store.

The interface is in English; to use it in Italian choose Settings › General › Language.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Requirements: Python 3.11+ (3.12 recommended) · macOS 12+ or Windows 10/11 with the Edge WebView2 runtime (already present on Windows 11).

macOSWindows 
git clone https://github.com/AleksAttanasio/ClusterSound.git && cd ClusterSound
uv venv -p 3.12 .venv && uv pip install -p .venv -e ".[dev]"
.venv/bin/python -m clustersound

git clone https://github.com/AleksAttanasio/ClusterSound.git; cd ClusterSound
py -3.12 -m venv .venv; .venv\Scripts\pip install -e ".[dev]"
.venv\Scripts\python -m clustersound

Without uv on macOS: python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -e ".[dev]".

docs.title: Ready-made app (macOS)
docs.text: Download the zip for your Mac (arm64 for Apple Silicon, x86_64 for Intel) from the Releases page: it contains ClusterSound.app with all the extras. The app is not notarized: open it the first time with right-click › Open.

docs.title: Optional extras
docs.text:
The heavy features are extras, to install only if you need them:

Extra Enables Command stems Extract stems in the Recorder (Demucs + PyTorch) pip install -e ".[stems]" enhance Enhance in the Recorder (Apollo + PyTorch) pip install -e ".[enhance]" midi Recording from a MIDI keyboard in Compose pip install -e ".[midi]" capture Recorder All outputs through ScreenCaptureKit (macOS, without the cs-tap helper) pip install -e ".[capture]"

The model weights of stems and enhance are downloaded by the app on first use (only once).

docs.title: Without the interface
docs.text:
.venv/bin/python -m clustersound --headless ~/Samples --out report.csv

Analyses the folder, prints the count per class and writes a CSV or JSON report.

Options: --debug opens the WebView inspector.

docs.title: Language
docs.text: The interface starts in English. To switch to Italian open Settings › General › Language: the app reloads in the chosen language and remembers it.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The Recorder records silence or does not see the outputs (macOS)

Grant System Audio Recording in System Settings → Privacy & Security. The cs-tap helper needs macOS 14.2+; without it only All outputs through ScreenCaptureKit is left (pip install -e ".[capture]"). Apps that protect their stream record silence on purpose.

On Windows the window stays white

Install the Microsoft Edge WebView2 runtime (already present on Windows 11).

On Windows the recording also contains ClusterSound's audio

It is a limit of WASAPI loopback: it cannot exclude a process. Stop the preview while you record.

Extract stems / Enhance say PyTorch is missing

Install the extra: pip install -e ".[stems]" or pip install -e ".[enhance]". On first use the app asks to download the weights (55 MB / 66 MB).

The Live device does not find the app

The app must be open: the bridge listens on 127.0.0.1:8770 (port in Settings › General). Check http://127.0.0.1:8770/live/ping in the browser.

A rack does not load in Live

Make sure ClusterSoundBridge is the Control Surface and read Live's Log.txt (~/Library/Preferences/Ableton/Live 10.x/Log.txt, ClusterSoundBridge lines). After an update run tools/install_live.sh again and restart Live.

The library says to press Rescan

At startup the app only restores from a snapshot; if the files changed, or the analysis version changed, a rescan is needed. Unchanged files come from the cache anyway.

The cache takes too much space

The online previews have a limit (300 MB, Settings › General › Temporary cache, with Clear). cache.sqlite holds the analyses: deleting it forces a new full analysis.

I want the interface in Italian

Settings › General › Language → Italiano. The app reloads in Italian; the choice is saved in settings.json.

docs.title: Manual
docs.text:
How to use every section of the app. The panel on the left groups the sections into Sample (Library, Store, Recorder) and Create (Sequencer, Drum Rack, Compose), with Settings at the bottom.

  • Interface — navigation, settings, flow between the sections.
  • Library — the 3D cloud, sample details, filters, corrections.
  • Store — free samples and packs from Freesound, Openverse, Internet Archive, ccMixter.
  • Recorder — records the audio output, slices, separates stems, restores with AI.
  • Sequencer — tries samples on 191 grooves in 47 genres and exports for Ableton.
  • Drum Rack — 8×8 kits for Launchpad and kits for the Roland SPD-SX.
  • Compose — chord progressions with suggestions and variations.
  • Melody — melodies, bass lines, arpeggios and riffs over the chords.
  • Max for Live — imports everything into Ableton Live without dragging files.

docs.title: Compose
docs.text: Builds chord progressions with the MIDI clips of a chord pack organised like the Unison MIDI Chord Pack (default ~/Documents/Unison MIDI Chord Pack; another folder in Settings › Compose). The pack is never modified: the files are read and indexed in memory.

docs.title: Chord browser
docs.text:
• The chords of the chosen key, grouped by degree (I, ii, bVII…) and coloured by function: green tonic, blue subdominant, orange dominant, purple colour/modal borrowing.
  • Triads, Extended, Borrowed & modal, Progressions filters and search by name or degree.
  • Click: listen · double-click, + or drag onto the timeline: add. The pack's progressions come in as one block per chord. Keys or categories missing from the pack are transposed from the nearest one.

docs.title: Key
docs.text:
• 🔒 Key: shows only the chords of that key; changing it transposes the whole progression.
  • Unlocked: chords from any key, each transposable ±12 semitones.
  • In both cases the key at the top is the reference for degrees and suggestions.

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text: Length in bars and grid (1 bar … 1/16) to choose. Drag a block to move it, its right edge to change its length: the following chords slide instead of overlapping. ⇔ Spread evenly gives all of them the same length. Every block shows the notes that really play (after strum, arpeggios and rhythm). Versions A, B, C… in the tabs above the timeline.

docs.title: Next chord
docs.text: Suggestions for the selected chord (or the last one), with a score and the reasons: harmonic function, cadences (V → I, ii → V, deceptive, plagal, bVI → bVII…), bass motion, common notes, voice leading and how often the move appears in the pack's progressions. If there is already a chord after the block, it also counts how well the suggestion leads into it. Under every proposal the colour variants of the same degree. Full formula in Algorithms › Harmony.

docs.title: Playing style
docs.text:
Per chord or as the default of the sequence (Mode):

  • Block, Strum (↑, ↓ or alternate, 5–80 ms), Arpeggio (up, down, up-down, random; 1/4…1/16 and triplets; 1–2 octaves);
  • Rhythm (quarter notes, eighth notes, offbeat, charleston, tresillo, syncopated house, half notes, pulse 1/16) played as block or strum;
  • note length, swing, dynamics curve, humanize (timing, velocity, feel, drift… 🎲 redraws it) and Alternation of styles on every hit or bar.

Preview and export use the same events, computed in Python.

docs.title: Variations
docs.text:
• Of a chord (✦ Vary harmony… or V): voicing (inversions, drop-2, open/close, doubled bass, minimal voice leading from the previous chord), colour (same degree, different extensions), substitutions in context, playing styles. ▶ plays the proposal from the bar before.
  • Of the progression (✦ on the version tab): reharmonisation (first and last chord stay), harmonic rhythm (anticipations, long-short, split chords), voice leading, richer / sparser, playing style and ending (IV → V, bVI → bVII, IV → iv, ii → V…), with a How much to vary slider. Keep saves it as a new version, Append adds it at the end.

docs.title: Exporting
docs.text:
• Export MIDI: one .mid (type 0, 480 PPQ, with the tempo) for the current version or one per version; chords only exports the block voicings without style. With a melody: Chords + melody (type 1), Chords only or Melody only.
  • Send to Live: Chords track with one clip per version, plus one track per melody layer.
  • Pattern: plays the progression together with the Sequencer pattern.
  • Save / Open… keep the progressions with all their versions; ⌘Z / ⇧⌘Z undo and redo.

Shortcuts: Space play/stop, ← → previous/next chord, Del delete, ⌘D duplicate, V variations.

docs.title: Drum Rack
docs.text: Builds kits of similar samples for two instruments: an 8×8 controller (Novation Launchpad Pro) or a Roland SPD-SX. The menu at the top left chooses the instrument; each one has its own kit.

docs.title: 8×8 controller
docs.text:
• Layouts: they split the 64 pads into groups of similar samples; the pads stay in place when the layout changes.
    • Columns ×8: 8 columns of 8 (e.g. all the hats on one column);
    • Blocks 2×2: 16 groups of 4;
    • Blocks 4×4: 4 quadrants of 16;
    • 4×4 in columns: every quadrant is a family, every column a group of 4;
    • Free: one pad at a time.
  • Note mapping (Settings › Drum Rack): Launchpad / Live (four 4×4 quadrants: 36–51 bottom left, 52–67 bottom right, 68–83 top left, 84–99 top right) or sequential rows (36 + row×8 + column) for Custom Modes.
  • Groups (panel on the right): family, choke group (on by default for the hats), 🔒 Lock group. Drag pads to swap them and a sample from the browser to put it on a pad; right-click = pad menu.

docs.title: Filling the groups
docs.text:
The seed is the last sample clicked (in the browser on the left, on a pad, or from the Library with Send → Drum Rack). Fill group puts the seed on the selected pad and similar samples on the other pads of the group.

Mode What it does Most similar the closest to the seed, without duplicates Random picks among the similar ones with a variation slider; Regenerate draws again Manual you tick the similar ones from a list sorted by similarity Trail uses the stops of the Library's Find similar, completed with the similar ones of the last stop
  • Similar among: same class as the seed, family of the group or the whole library; One-shots only; Avoid samples already in the kit.
  • Auto-fill: fills the empty groups by family (Alt+click regenerates every unlocked one).
  • 🎲 Random: every unlocked group takes a random group of similar samples of its family; it can be limited to a folder or pack, to one-shots, and match the dynamics.

docs.title: Roland SPD-SX
docs.text:
• Pads drawn as on the instrument: 1–3 at the top, 4–9 below, plus Pedal (Trig 1) and Trig 2, turned on with their tick. The pedal gets a kick; without the pedal the kick goes on pad 8.
  • Factory MIDI notes: pads 1–9 = 60–68, Trig 1 = 69, Trig 2 = 70.
  • Configurations: Classic kit, Rows, Columns, Cross, Percussion, Free.
  • Playability: at most 2 kicks (pedal + 1 pad), 3 snares/claps and 5 among hats and cymbals. The families that would exceed the limits are disabled; if the kit exceeds them a warning appears.
  • 🎲 Generate kit: a random playable configuration, with every group taken from a group of sounds that no one else uses (the pedal kick and a pad kick sound different).

docs.title: Exporting and using
docs.text:
• → Sequencer: loads the samples into the Sequencer buses by class, up to 8 per bus; choose which buses, whether to overwrite/add/clear the others, and the alternation (default random, except kick, FX and bass).
  • Export for Ableton (8×8): Samples/<group>/<note> - <name>.wav, … Drum Rack.adg (Launchpad notes and choke groups), .license.txt of the online samples and README.txt with the pad map.
  • Export (Live + SPD-SX): … SPD-SX Drum Rack.adg on the SPD-SX notes, the SPD-SX/ folder with 16-bit / 44.1 kHz WAVs (P1 - … … T2 - …) to import with SPD-SX Wave Manager, and README.txt.
  • Send to Live, Save / Load kit.

How the samples are chosen: Algorithms › Drum Rack.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
• Navigation: the panel on the left lists the sections; the button next to the logo collapses it to icons only. The Library shows the number of analysed samples; the Recorder a red dot while it records.
  • Settings: the fine-tuning options of every section (folders, formats, devices, MIDI mappings…) are gathered in Settings, split by section and saved straight away. The ⋯ button at the top right of every screen opens the matching section directly.
  • The sections talk to each other: a sample from the Library or the Store goes to the Sequencer or the Drum Rack with the Send menu (right-click on a 3D point or a row); the Drum Rack loads its samples into the Sequencer buses; the Recorder sends regions to the Drum Rack; Compose plays together with the Sequencer pattern; everything can be sent to Ableton Live.
  • No file is modified: the app only writes in its own folders (data, cache, ~/Music/ClusterSound …).
Settings › General Language interface language: English (default) or Italiano; the app reloads to apply it Ableton Live bridge port of the local server for the device (default 8770) Temporary cache limit of the online previews and of the samples tried (default 300 MB), Clear

The other settings are described on the page of each section; the full list is in Reference › Settings. The shortcuts are in Reference › Shortcuts.

Windows

Everything works as on the Mac: shortcuts with Ctrl instead of ⌘, Show in folder opens File Explorer, the window uses Edge WebView2. Reserved names (CON, NUL, COM1…) get a _ in front.

docs.title: Library
docs.text: The Library analyses a folder of samples (recursively), assigns every file to one of the 34 classes and shows the whole library as a 3D cloud: similar sounds sit close together, the colour of a point is its class.

docs.title: Folder and scan
docs.text:
• Choose folder… (from the empty library or from Settings › Library): wav, aif, flac, ogg, mp3, caf, w64 formats.
  • The results go into a cache: a Rescan only reads new or modified files again. At startup the last folder is restored from a snapshot without analysing anything again.
  • Store downloads saved inside the library folder are added with an automatic rescan.

docs.title: 3D view
docs.text:
• Drag to rotate, scroll to zoom, right-click to pan. At the bottom: auto-rotate, reset view, class labels on/off.
  • Click on a point: immediate playback and the detail drawer opens.
  • Double-click: Find similar on that sample.
  • Right-click: Send menu (Sequencer, Drum Rack).

docs.title: Detail drawer
docs.text:
• Dynamics: waveform with the RMS envelope in dB and the estimated ADSR phases.
  • Spectrogram: click to play from that point.
  • Measures: duration, peak, RMS, crest, attack, decay, sustain, release, T60, format, channels/bit, type, centroid, harmonicity, subcluster.
  • Class and alternatives: the most likely classes with their confidence.
  • Actions: Play, Show in folder, Find similar, Send ▾, More in the Store (opens the Store on the same class).

docs.title: Correcting a class
docs.text: Change the class from the Class menu of the drawer: the sample becomes a training example and within a few seconds every other classification is updated (the library head is retrained). Manual labels stay in the cache and survive rescans. See Classifier.

docs.title: Find similar
docs.text:
Shows the closest samples (cosine similarity on the YAMNet embeddings) laid out around the centre, with the similarity percentage. The slider chooses how many to show (5–60).

  • Click listens, double-click re-centres on the sample: the stops form a trail, which the Drum Rack can use to fill a group (Trail).
  • ▦ Drum Rack fills the selected group with the similar samples; Exit goes back to the cloud.

docs.title: Filters and list
docs.text:
• Class: click to turn on/off, Alt+click = only that one; All · None.
  • Type: One-shot, Loop, Long/Texture.
  • Minimum confidence and search by name or folder.
  • List: sortable table; ↑ ↓ move and listen.

docs.title: Export report
docs.text:
Settings › Library › Export report: CSV or JSON with path, class, confidence, alternatives, subcluster and type of every sample. The same report can be produced without the GUI with --headless.

Shortcuts: Space play/stop, Esc closes the drawer.

docs.title: Max for Live
docs.text: The ClusterSound device (MIDI effect, Live 10.1 Suite or later) imports patterns, sequences, drum racks and progressions into the set, without dragging files. Installation: Quick start › Ableton Live.

docs.title: Importing
docs.text:
With the app open:

  • From the device: choose the kind (saved patterns, sequences, drum racks, progressions) and the item, then Import. Refresh reads the catalogue again.
    • a pattern creates the Drums and Bass tracks, each with its own rack and clip;
    • a sequence does the same with a clip as long as the sequence;
    • a drum rack creates a track with the rack;
    • a progression creates a Chords track (one clip per version) and a Melody track if there is one.
  • From the app: Send to Live in the Sequencer, in the sequence bar, in the Drum Rack, in the Recorder and in Compose's Export menu. With Receive on the device imports straight away, even what is not saved.
  • Clip → Melody: sends the notes of the selected MIDI clip to the app (Compose → Melody → Import ▾ → Clip from Ableton).

Rules: New tracks (default) creates them after the selected one; Tempo sets the BPM of the set; the clips start from the selected scene and always go into an empty slot, without overwriting anything. Without the Remote Script the clips are created anyway and the device shows the rack to drag from the browser.

docs.title: Trying Live instruments
docs.text:
In the right column of the device:

  • Track: the tracks of the last import; for Drums also an entry per bus (Drums › Kick…).
  • Type: the categories of Live's Sounds (Bass, Pad, Piano & Keys, Synth Lead…), the drum kits, the presets of every instrument (Operator, Wavetable, Analog…) and, for the buses, the hits of that bus.
  • Instrument: the presets of the type, 60 at a time. Choosing one, or scrolling with ◀ ▶, loads it and starts the clip in a loop; Try ▶ loads it again, Stop stops.
  • ★ ClusterSound sample (or ClusterSound kit) puts the app's samples back.

Tracks that arrive without an instrument get the first preset of their type (Piano & Keys for the chords, Bass for the bass, a kit for the drums), so every import plays straight away.

docs.title: Sequences and kits
docs.text:
Saving a sequence also saves the Sequencer kit, and the device imports it with that kit. For older sequences it uses the user pattern of the first block, or only the MIDI ((MIDI only)) if the block comes from a genre preset; failing that it uses the kit open now ((current kit)).

If something does not load, the reason is in the device status and in Live's Log.txt (ClusterSoundBridge lines). Protocol and architecture: Technical › Live integration.

docs.title: Melody
